schools.summary: Henry reads thunder and lightning as sensible indications of God's glory and terror — one to the ear, one to the eye — designed to awaken the slumbering world, and the proper preface, as on Sinai, to the voice about to break out at ch. 38.
Gill hears a trembling of reverence at God's majesty, recalling Sinai where Moses feared and quaked, and thinks Elihu is watching a real storm gather as he speaks.
Clarke: a proper view of God's majesty in the thunder appalls the stoutest heart; he protests only that the chapter division here is absurd.
Ellicott keeps it vivid — not the cattle only, but Elihu's own heart trembles and is moved out of its place: 'Hark! listen to the sound of His voice.'

outliers.note: Protests that the chapter division is absurd — this storm-piece, to the middle of v.5, belongs with the close of the preceding chapter.

themes: thunder as the voice of God
ear and eye the learning senses

schools.summary: Clarke renders the doubled Hebrew 'hear with hearing' and takes it of a real tempest breaking over the house, the peals rolling and lightning flashing until Elihu finished and God spoke from the storm; Wesley: the thunder is God's voice, produced by his word and command.

Keil and Delitzsch read the doubled verb as attentive hearing, note the fivefold 'voice' recalling the sevenfold voice of Psalm 29, and grant a copyist may have added that the lightning flashes and thunder rolls.
Gill takes the thunder as God's voice in the clouds and hears Elihu, affected himself, exhorting the company to hearken and learn.

themes: hear attentively the noise of his voice
the sound out of his mouth

schools.summary: Clarke fixes on the speed — the lightning directed east to west in the twinkling of an eye, its light reaching earth's ends so a hemisphere sees it at once; Wesley: God guides his voice like an arrow to the mark to do the work he sends it for.

Gill has the thunder roll from one end of heaven to the other, God charging the clouds where to strike and where the rain shall fall — against Pliny's 'chance' — and turns it to the ministers of the word directed where to fall with power.
Ellicott prefers 'sendeth it forth,' referring the 'it' to the noise and rumbling that fills all heaven rather than to the bolt alone.

themes: he directeth it under the whole heaven
lightning to the ends of the earth

schools.summary: Gill explains flash-before-clap by the quicker sense of sight and quicker motion of light, and makes the roaring thunder an emblem of the law's thunder and the awakening sound of the gospel preached by the sons of thunder.

Clarke renders 'the voice of his excellency' as 'of his majesty' — no sound so becomes God as thunder — and reads 'he will not stay them' as the lightnings unlimited and unbounded, like God, irresistible.
Ellicott reads 'he stayeth them not' as none being able to track the thunder and lightning, which travel in paths none can explore.
Henry takes it that God need not check or restrain them but lets them run their course, or else that he will not stay the rains that follow the thunder.

debates.question: How is 'he will not stay them when his voice is heard' to be understood?

sides.position: God does not limit or circumscribe the lightnings, which light the whole world unbounded and irresistible
none can track the thunder and lightning, which travel in paths none can explore
God need not restrain them but lets them run their course, or will not stay the rains that follow

schools.summary: Gill takes 'marvellously' of the marvellous effects of the bolt — rending rocks, felling towers and oaks, the strange reports of egg, cask, coin, and womb spared or struck — and hears the gospel voice thundering out its wonders of Trinity and redemption.

Clarke makes the verse the true close of the storm-piece, sets beside it the thunderstorm of Psalm 77:16-19, and marks 'great things doeth he' as a fresh paragraph opening onto snow, frost, and cloud.

Henry makes the verse a rebuke of irreligious weather-talk: God commissions the snow where to light and how long to lie, and saying and doing are not two things with him; it is sin to contend with his providence in the weather.

Clarke turns naturalist on the crystalline six-pointed flakes and the snow's use in covering the tender plants, reshaping the verse with Mr. Good; Wesley glosses the 'great rain of his strength' as storms of irresistible violence.

Gill dwells on the literal 'be thou earth,' sets aside the rabbinic fancy of earth made from snow, and counts the snow among God's incomprehensible works — cold yet warming, falling even in hot lands.
Ellicott: every operation of nature — snow, gentle shower, drenching downpour — obeys God's behest, who by them seals up men's hands that all may learn they are not the free agents they suppose.

themes: he saith to the snow, Be thou on the earth
saying and doing one with God

schools.summary: Clarke reads the sealing of the hand as the work of the frost, binding men's labour till the thaw; Wesley: by snow and rain God drives men from the fields and binds their hands, that they may contemplate his works.

Gill takes the sealing as a shutting up of labour — traveller, craftsman, and husbandman all stopped — and notes Sephorno's turn that the increase gathered into men's hands leads them to love and fear God.
Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the head of the winter panel and weigh the difficult word the versions split between 'chosen,' 'grain,' and 'brightness,' keeping it near its root with Schultens.

outliers.note: Digresses to denounce the folly of chiromancy built on this verse's 'seal upon the hand,' citing the great folio a Cologne scholar filled with palm-reading.

themes: he sealeth up the hand of every man
that all may know his work

schools.summary: Gill takes it of the wild beasts, which when snow and rain lie thick betake themselves to their dens to lurk and lie in wait for prey.
Ellicott draws the parallel that gives the verse its point: not man only but the beasts likewise must take refuge in their dens and coverts.
Henry: the winter drives men and beasts alike to retire — the wild by instinct, the tame by man's care as in Exod. 9:20 — and asks whether man alone shall be without an ark.
Gill weighs 'chamber' (the inside of the cloud, or God's treasury) against 'south,' and settles on 'south,' the quarter these lands knew the whirlwind to come from.
Clarke refers to his note on Job 9:9 where the word is 'chambers,' cites the Chaldee 'from the supreme chamber the commotion,' and guesses the whirlwind a scorching blast like the simoom.
Ellicott renders 'out of its chamber cometh the whirlwind,' the typhoon, and 'cold from the northern constellations.'
Henry reads 'out of the hidden place,' refusing 'south' precisely because v.17 makes the south wind a warming and quieting one, not a whirlwind.

debates.question: Does the whirlwind come 'out of the south' or 'out of the (hidden) chamber'?

sides.position: out of the south, the quarter these lands knew the whirlwind from
out of the hidden chamber or storehouse of the winds

themes: out of the south cometh the whirlwind

schools.summary: Clarke owns the freezing of water still a mystery fit for the 'great things we cannot comprehend,' marvels at its expansive power splitting metal, and reads the second clause with Mr. Good of the frozen surface as a mirror; Wesley: the waters are bound up in crystal fetters.
Gill reads 'the breath of God' as his word and command, or a mighty freezing north wind, the divine name enlarging the thing (so Sephorno).
Ellicott glosses the straitened waters as 'firm, like a molten mass' — the flowing water arrested and made solid at a breath.

themes: by the breath of God frost is given
the breadth of the waters straitened

schools.summary: Wesley: the clouds spend themselves wearied watering the earth, and the bright clouds God scatters by wind or sun; Clarke prefers 'the brightness dissipates the cloud,' the bright sunshine wearing out the thick cloud, but allows the received sense.

Ellicott gives 'He ladeth the thick cloud with moisture' and 'scattereth the cloud of his lightning,' but sets beside it 'the bright sun weareth out the thick cloud'; Keil and Delitzsch render 'He loadeth the clouds with water, he spreadeth far the cloud of his light.'
Gill takes it plainly — God loads and wearies the cloud by filling it with waters, then drains it, an emblem of ministers who spend and are spent — noting Broughton's 'fair weather.'

debates.question: What does 'by watering he wearieth the thick cloud' describe?

sides.position: God wearies and empties the cloud by watering the earth from it
the brightness or the bright sun wears out and disperses the thick cloud
God loads the thick cloud with moisture and spreads his lightning-cloud abroad

themes: by watering he wearieth the thick cloud
God charges and discharges the cloud

schools.summary: Gill reads the cloud driven by the wind, turned to every point of the compass by the will of God, who sits at the helm and orders all by the counsel of his own will.
Wesley: the clouds are carried about not by chance, though nothing seems more casual, but by God's order and governance.
Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as the turn toward Job's instruction — the man who would dictate to God is bidden stand still, that the clouds execute all he commands over the wide earth.

outliers.note: Reads the verse of the sun rather than the cloud — the sun revolving on its axis and holding the planets by attraction as by a cable — but half-retracts it as perhaps too far-fetched.

themes: turned round about by his counsels

schools.summary: Clarke unfolds the three ends — 'correction' (a rod, inundating floods), 'his land' (Palestine, his favoured people), and 'mercy' (fertilizing showers to a wasted district) — with the Vulgate and a glance at the flood; Wesley divides them the same way, reaching even to the universal deluge.
Gill notes simply that it is the cloud and its rain that God causes to come.
Henry presses the moral: the same rain, by its measure, is either a great judgment or a great mercy, made to fall on one city and not another (Amos 4:7).

themes: for correction, or his land, or mercy
judgment and mercy by the same means

schools.summary: Henry makes the verse the doorway to all that follows: what we hear profits us only if we stand still and consider, and Elihu's whole design is the humbling of Job, ignorant of the divine mechanics and so no judge of the divine politics.

Clarke sharpens each verb — hear, stand still, consider — and dwells on the 'wondrous works' endless in variety and incomprehensible in their making; Wesley argues from the lesser to the greater: if the obvious works so wonder us, how wonderful his secret counsels.
Gill points the summons at the clouds of correction or mercy: Job is to apply it and consider whether his afflictions are for reproof or in love, since both might be.

Clarke reports that almost every critic understands 'the light of his cloud' of the rainbow, the bow of Genesis 9:13; Wesley agrees it is probably the rainbow, in a cloud that may be called God's because in it he set his bow.

Ellicott takes 'the light of his cloud' of the lightning — the secrets of God's thunderbolts — though he records the guess that it means the sun dispersing the cloud; Keil and Delitzsch keep the clause temporal, 'dost thou know when God disposed them.'
Gill takes the clouds as the works in view — decreed, stored, disposed, ordered where to fall — and asks how a man ignorant of these can claim to know the springs of providence.

debates.question: What is 'the light of his cloud'?

sides.position: the rainbow, the sign of Genesis 9 that the earth shall not again be drowned
the lightning hidden in the cloud (or, alternatively, the sun that disperses it)

themes: dost thou know when God disposed them

schools.summary: Clarke sets the wonder in his own science — evaporation and the gravity of the air bearing up such weights of vapour — and prefers Mr. Good's 'Wonders, perfections of wisdom!'; Wesley: God weighs the clouds in his balances, held up by the thin air.
Gill puts the wonder as weight — how those ponderous water-laden bodies are so poised that they hang without tilting or falling.
Ellicott glosses the balancings as the clouds poised and suspended in the sky, quoting Coleridge's 'Ye clouds, that far above me float and pause.'

Clarke turns the plain question into a confession of ignorance — what are warmth and cold? — explaining that garments only hinder the escape of natural heat, yet why north brings cold and south heat he cannot demonstrate; Wesley: the air made calm and warm by the sun in the southern quarter.

Ellicott offers 'when the earth is still,' of the sultry calm; Keil and Delitzsch read the particle as 'that' not 'how,' carrying the sentence into v.18, addressing Job as the man 'whose garments became hot when the land is sultry from the south.'
Gill grants the plain sense — clothes warm in summer under the south wind — yet insists a concourse of Providence and blessing is needed, without which the garment would not warm the man.

themes: the south wind quiets the earth

schools.summary: Clarke turns the verse into a hymn to the world's fitness — the expanse, the weight fitted to the winds, the air's gravity and elasticity, the heaven a polished metal reflecting images; Wesley: the sky thin yet firm, a molten glass of brass and steel, smooth and without flaw.

Ellicott renders 'hast thou spread out with him the magnificent dome of heaven,' noting the words imply the cloud-covered sky, so the sun may be the hidden subject; Keil and Delitzsch open the final strophe here — he who censures God injures himself.
Gill takes it as a challenge to Job's presumption: was he an assistant in the first spreading of the sky? God spread it as a canopy without another's help.

themes: hast thou with him spread out the sky
no hand in the making of the world

schools.summary: Clarke hears a biting irony at Job's pretensions — make us as wise as thyself, that we too may approach God's boldness; for our part we are wrapped in darkness — and notes Mr. Good's 'when arrayed in robes of darkness'; Wesley makes the darkness double, of the matter and of our minds.
Gill reads a confession of how ill men are fitted to reason with the wonder-working God about providence, when they know so little of his common works; let Job teach them how.

outliers.note: Takes the 'him' to be the sun, hidden behind the clouds and not gone but still there — the distinctive thread he carries through vv.18-21, where the others read God.

themes: teach us what we shall say unto him
darkness of the matter and the mind

schools.summary: Clarke sets Elihu's fear against Job's rashness — shall I dare whisper before God, and how could I stand? — then turns on Job, who arraigned God's government and all but charged him with cruelty; Wesley reads the swallowing up as the effect of God's infinite majesty on any who challenge him.

Gill hears a man asking whether his imperfect words are worth relating to the omniscient God, and God forbid it should be reported that Elihu spoke as Job did; notes Broughton's 'shall it be recorded.'
Ellicott lets the sense vary with the subject — of God, awe at his majesty; of the sun, whether any ever said the sun is swallowed up and extinguished.

themes: shall it be told him that I speak
surely he shall be swallowed up
the nearer to God, the less one dares

schools.summary: Clarke reads it of the insufferable brightness of the sun in a wind-swept sky — who can gaze at it, much less at God? — through Mr. Good; Wesley takes the light for the sun, unseeable when the sky is very clear, so no wonder we cannot see God.
Gill sifts lightning, rainbow, and Milky Way and settles on the sun, hidden by clouds till the wind sweeps them, or shining in full strength too bright to look upon.

Henry hears Elihu watching a real sky — God advancing in an awful chariot of cloud (2 Chron. 6:1), the light hidden as the disciples feared in the cloud (Luke 9:34), yet the north clearing as the wind dried Noah's flood (Gen. 8:1).

Ellicott makes the verse the threshold of the theophany: the sun bright behind the clouds comes forth like gold when the north wind clears them, but upon God is terrible majesty — the hidden sun we shall see again, but who shall find out God?

themes: men see not the bright light
the sun as a parable of the hidden God

schools.summary: Clarke defends the literal 'gold' with Calmet (gold from Colchis, Armenia, Ophir, all north countries) and ties it to the terrible majesty — as gold from the north, so praise with fear and trembling; Wesley keeps to the weather, the northern winds clearing the sky, Elihu speaking in haste as God draws near.
Gill notes the word is literally 'gold' — some take it strictly of the metal from the north — but leans to the figurative serenity of the air, bright as gold, Broughton's 'golden weather.'
Keil and Delitzsch render it flatly of the metal, 'gold is brought from the north,' set against 'above Eloah is terrible majesty.'

debates.question: Does the verse speak of 'fair weather' or 'gold' out of the north?

sides.position: gold, the metal brought from the northern lands
fair weather, the golden serenity of the cleared sky

themes: fair weather cometh out of the north

schools.summary: Henry reads a chain of glories — past finding out, excellent in power, no less in wisdom and justice, so that he who can do everything will do everything for the best, and will not afflict willingly or beyond what is needful.

Wesley keeps 'he will not afflict without just cause,' being excellent in power he can do no unrighteous act; but Clarke breaks with the rendering, taking the Hebrew as 'he will not answer' — God gives account of none of his matters to us.
Gill dwells on the name Almighty — nothing impossible, all-sufficient, needing nothing his creatures can give.
Ellicott reads the verse of a God mighty in power and justice, leaving the crux where he finds it.

debates.question: Does the last clause mean 'he will not afflict' or 'he will not answer'?

sides.position: he will not afflict beyond just cause, considering our frame
he will not answer, giving account of none of his matters to us

themes: he will not afflict or he will not answer

schools.summary: Clarke sharpens the last clause into the humbling of pride — no man valuable for his wisdom, whatever good in him God's own, let him that glorieth glory in the Lord — and marks the theophany breaking in, God answering from the whirlwind; Wesley: reverence and submission, the 'wise of heart' being the wise in their own eyes.
Gill gathers the grounds of fear from God's power, judgment, justice, and goodness, and concludes men should reverence, submit, and serve him with godly fear.
Ellicott hears a wordplay between fearing and seeing, rendering 'men may fear him, but none even of the wise in heart shall see him,' though granting the Authorized reading the more literal.

debates.question: How is 'he respecteth not any that are wise of heart' to be read?

sides.position: God pays no regard to those who are wise in their own conceit
not even the wise in heart shall see him (a wordplay on fear and see)

themes: he respecteth not the wise of heart
the fear of God as wisdom's end
the stage cleared for God to speak
